title: Pre-Civil War New Orleans as America's musical center
summary: New Orleans led the nation musically; the French Opera toured northern cities and introduced instruments.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Well, what about the rest of the country, as compared with New Orleans, as far as general musical sophistication is concerned? Both Negro and white, I'm talking about.

Well, it depends on the period you're talking about. In the, uh, pre-Civil War period, New Orleans is unmistakably miles ahead of the rest of the United States. It is a musical center in the United States. No question about that. And, uh, this was not exclusive with the whites. There were a great many Negro musicians who were taught by the white musicians playing in the French Opera, and in, uh, uh, the St. Charles Theater Orchestra, which was a very, very fine orchestra, uh, also. And these Negro musicians, in turn, were often employed as teachers for the children of, uh, white families. Quite a, quite a lot of musical, uh, interchange there. And, uh, either for these orchestras or for the opera, or for the general musical environment, no, no other city in pre-Civil War, United States came up to New Orleans. Even Boston. Even Boston. When the, uh, when the French Opera here went on tour, and it toured from 1827 to 1833, with the exception of one year, 1832, when the cholera epidemic was very strong in all the country, uh, north as well as south. And, uh, six of those seven years, the French Opera was on tour. They introduced, uh, uh, many things to Boston. They, they gave Boston, in fact, probably its, uh, first taste of opera like that. And they, they toured, not, not in every year did they hit all these cities, but in various years, they hit Boston, New York, Philadelphia, and Baltimore. And, uh, they did a great deal to revive all interest in opera in those cities. After all, the, many books will say that the first opera in the United States, uh, to amount to anything, uh, was the presentation by a Garcia troupe in New York City in 1825 of, uh, uh, Rossini's, uh, Barbara Seville. And that had played in its entirety here in 1823, two years earlier. And this company went on tour to New York in 27, just two years after the Garcia troupe. And the reviews uniformly appraised this as being a better ensemble, a better organized opera company. Uh, at a time when a lot of the instruments were either totally unknown or very little known in northern cities, this orchestra here, which was over 35 pieces or so, and had such instruments as bassoons and oboes, introduced these instruments in many of these cities. And when you come to, uh, post-Civil War, of course, you have the reconstruction problems, which hit New Orleans heavily up until 1876 or so. Uh, but the, uh, general interest in music and in parades, uh, was so persistent that it lasted well into the post-war period. Not long ago I heard a man visiting New Orleans, and he used a phrase, which is a rather good phrase for the city. He said that every time he came to New Orleans, and this is in the 1950s now, every time he came to New Orleans, he always found the city halfway between a ball and a parade. And I think it was always that way.
But they had academic music games, they mostly in the form of opera? That was the principal academic music, opera.
